ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Effect of Price Hike of PDS Commodities in Kerala 
*561. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN : Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Kerala Chief Minister has submitted any representation to 
the Central Government regarding the hardships being faced by the people of 
Kerala because of the recent hike in prices of PDS articles; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action taken in this regard ? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) to (c) A statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) Yes Sir. 
(b) Chief Minister, Kerala, has stated that the State is deficit in 
foodgrains production, and that the hike in Central Issue prices of wheat and 
rice will destroy the Statutory Public Distribution System. He has appealed to 
the Union Government to withdraw the decision since Kerala is heavily 
dependant on the Public Distribu tion System for supply of essential 
commodities. 
(c) Chief Minister, Kerala, has been informed that the recent 
modifications in the Targeted Public Distribution System have been made in 
order to focus attention on the poor and channelise the resources to the 
targeted group. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [05 MAY, 2000] 
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN : Mr. Chairman, Sir, this is a serious 
issue relating to the State of Kerala, a State which is producing only one -third 
of its total need of foodgrains and is highly dependant on the Publ ic 
Distribution System for allotment of rice and wheat from the Central Pool. 
The record shows that the State of Kerala was the first on the PDS list. We 
have 15,000 ration shops and 80 per cent of the need is catered through the 
Public Distribution System . The State is facing a serious problem because of 
the recent decision of the Government of India to increase the PDS prices, 
especially under the BPL and the APL mechanism. That was why the Chief 
Minister of Kerala himself had led a dharna in Delhi, and after that, he met 
the Prime Minister and submitted a representation. Because of that, I put this 
question. But the reply does not reveal anything positive for the State. After 
this decision, the offtake has also come down. Normally, we need 1,45,000 
tonnes of rice and the averge offtake is 1,20,000 tonnes. Because of this 
decision, the offtake has been reduced to 30,000 tonnes. In such a situation, 
two questions have been posed by the State Government The first is regarding 
the below poverty line people. Th e State Government has conducted a survey 
through the village panchayat system and it was proved that 42 per cent of the 
people are living below poverty line. The Central Government is covering 
only 25 per cent of them through their allotment. Will the Cen tral 
Government allot the targeted thing, that is, the TDPS to 42 per cent of the 
families which have been surveyed by the village panchayat system ? 
Secondly, the State of Kerala is only producing one -third of its need. So, 
there is a shortage unlike the other southern States, will the Central 
Government consider the case of Kerala and the north eastern parts of the 
country separately while fixing the prices of the essential commodities under 
the PDS ?

American help for Environment Protection 
†562. SHRl SWARAJ KAUSHAL . Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that America has assured to help India in the 
protection of environment; 
(b) if so, the details of thereof; 
(c) whether any agreement has been signed for this purpose; and 
(d) if so, the main features thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) to (d) A Joint Statement on Co -operation in Energy and 
Environment between India and the United States of America was signed on 
22-3-2000. The objective of the Joint Statement is to intensif y further co -
operation in the fields of clean energy and environmental protection. 
The Joint Statement expresses the intention of the two countries to 
create a Joint Consultative Committee to foster greater bilateral cooperation, 
Government-to-Government d ialogue and further encourage public and 
private sector cooperation in these sectors. The Joint Consultative Group will 
(a) identify, initiate and monitor public and private collaborative projects in 
research, development, transfer, demonstration and deplo yment of 
appropriate technologies and review policies in the areas of clean energy, 
renewable energy, energy efficiency and power sector reform, (b) explore 
and expand opportunities for commercial development and cooperation in 
clean energy, and (c) enhance cooperation on climate change issues that arise 
in the context of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate 
Change. 
SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL : Mr. Chairman, Sir, through you, may I 
ask the Hon. Minister as to whether we propose to accept the clean 
development mechanism, which means that India will have to reduce the 
carbon dioxide emission level, although it is America which is the biggest 
emitter of carbon dioxide. How do you reduce those carbon dioxide 
emissions ? It can be done only by reducing our  industrial activity. What I 
want to know from the Hon. Minister is, do we propose to accept the clean 
development mechanism ? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [05 MAY, 2000] 
SHRI T. R BAALU : Mr. Chairman, Sir, actually India's approach to 
CDM is, there should be environmental integrity, climate change 
effectiveness, conformity with sustainable development, priorities of India, 
principles and rules must conform to equity and principles of common but 
differentiated responsibilities, voluntary participation. Sir, actually, the clean 
development mechanism is our choice. Whatever technology that has to be 
got from other nations, whether it is from the developed countries or others, 
it is our choice. On the transfer of tech nology, we have got our own option. 
But, at the same time, the technology and the process should be 
environmentally sustainable. This is our priority. 
SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL : Sir, the answer of the Minister is very 
vague. What we wanted to know was that alth ough America is the biggest 
emitter of carbon dioxide, does this mechanism, the CDM, mean that we 
alone will have to reduce the carbon dioxide levels; if so, how do we reduce 
the carbon dioxide levels ? This can be done only by reducing the industrial 
activity. Only we are obliged, or, America is also obliged to reduce the 
carbon dioxide level ? That is precisely what I want to know. 
SHRI T. R. BAALU: America and other developed countries have got 
a mechanism. They can fund technology to the developing countries and they 
can have their emission certificate. The second option is, between the 
developed countries, they can have the project -based emission reduction. The 
third option is, they can transfer the emission from developed countries to 
other developed c ountries. At the same time, we can select our own option, 
we can select our own technology. It is for us to see whether it suits our 
country. 
SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Sir, on this issue, India has 
been taking a consistent stand, alongwith several devel oping countries, with 
regard to environmental degradation, depletion of the ozone layer and such 
other issues. Our position is that the primary responsibility for the 
environmental degradation rests with the developed countries and they 
should take up the major share for setting the environment into the right path. 
I want to know from the Hon. Minister whether India has changed its 
consistent position which we have been taking, alongwith other countries on 
this issue, by signing this agreement ? 
SHRI T. R. BAALU : The Hon. Member is very correct. The primary 
responsibility rests with the developed countries. Sir, we have got no target at 
all. We did not change our attitude even during the last conference held in 
New York. I have emphasised and re -emphasised that the developing 
countries, 
10

including India, have got no target. We are not having an obligation or 
having any target. At the same time, the developed countries have to reduce, 
for instance, the USA. They have to reduce seven per cent of the 1990 level 
by 2012. These are the targets that have been fixed; between reduction eight 
and increase limit to ten per cent, for the developed countries, as per the UN 
Convention. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL : Sir, the real impact of the question i s that under 
the Kyoto Protocol, to which India is not a party, if the United States, which 
is a party to the Kyoto Protocol, persuades India and enters into an 
agreement for purposes of reduction of levels of carbon dioxide, then the 
United States gets cr edit for it under the Kyoto Protocol. So, arc we, by 
entering into such an agreement with the United States, somehow indirectly 
benefiting the United States in terms of the Kyoto Protocol ? That is the 
question. 
SHRI T. R. BAALU : Not at all, Sir. My frien d, a learned lawyer, has 
mentioned that India is not a party to the Protocol so far But, even the United 
States has not yet ratified the Kyoto Protocol. More than 180 countries are 
parties to the convention. We arc waiting for discussions to progress to 
endorse the Protocol. The United States hasn't ratified it. Many of the 
developing countries have not endorsed the Kyoto Protocol. But, finally 
various issues have to be considered by 2000. By the end of this year, every 
country that is party to the conventi on, has to take decision on issues about 
Kyoto Protocol. There is a discussion going on. At the same time, we have 
got no obligation at all. We have signed the UN Convention on Climate 
change. We are party to that. Under the Kyoto Protocol, discussions are 
going on in the multilateral fora. In the last week's meeting also, we have 
emphasised that India has got no obligation on emission reduction targets. 
For instance, the average per capita emission in the world is 1.2 tonnes, 
whereas the average per capita emission in India is 0.2 tonnes only. We have 
got no obligation at all, as it is.

SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Sir, this is a question of concept. The 
retention price scheme itself was devised in 1977. The payment is being made 
to fertilizer companies for the last 23 years based on their actually claiming 
whatever expenditure is incurred by them on two accounts. One is the capital 
related charges which are fixed charges. The related charges include 
depreciation, return on the capital employed, network and other issues that 
are capital-related charges. The other is the actual operating charges, charges 
on account of feed stock, conversion charges and selling and administrative 
expenses. Besides that, the Government also pays the transport subsidy 
because, as I said earlier, fertilizers are sold at a uniform price throughout the 
country because a single farm -gate price has been determined. Therefore, the 
transport amount is paid. All these components vary from one company to 
another, depending upon the technology used and variou s other issues,

the system suffers from several aberrations and infirmities, that includes this,

THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SURESH PRABHU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. DAP has been decontrolled since 
24-8-1992 and its imports have been decanalized with effect from 17 -9-1992. 
However, the Government determines the Maximum Retail Prices (MRP) 
and the rates of Concession for indigenous and imported DAP under the 
Concession Scheme of the Department of Agricul ture and Cooperation. The 
indigenous producers of DAP are at a disadvantage as the raw 
materials/intermediates required for its production are not available in the 
country. To compensate for this disadvantage, rate of concession for 
indigenous DAP is pegge d at a higher level than that of imported DAP. For 
1999-2000, the Government had fixed concession of Rs. 4600 per metric 
tonne (provisional) for indigenous DAP and Rs. 3200 per metric tonne for 
imported DAP. At these rates of concession, indigenous product ion has been 
38.58 lakh metric tonnes which is higher than the target of 37.25 lakh metric 
tonnes for 1999- 2000. Imports in the same period have been nearly 33 lakh 
metric tonnes. Thus the domestic production has not suffered despite the high 
level of imports. 
In the market place both indigenous and imported DAP are sold at a 
competitive price. The Government role is to put in place the policy which 
spurs both the indigenous production and imports. The selling price to 
fanners is a function of demand and supply. 
The Government has not received any representation regarding 
dumping of DAP by foreign suppliers in the country nor has the industry 
been of the view that there has been dumping of DAP.

disincentives; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) and (b) The 
National Population Policy, 2000 has been approved by the Government 
during February, 2000. It was laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha on 7th 
March, 2000. The Policy  affirms the commitment of government towards 
voluntary and informed choice and consent of citizens while availing of 
reproductive health care services, and continuation of the target free approach 
in administering family planning services. The NPP 2000 pr ovides a policy 
framework for advancing goals and prioritizing strategies during the next 
decade, to meet the reproductive and child health needs of the people of 
India, and to achieve net replacement level of fertility (TFR) by 2010. It is 
based upon the need to simultaneously address issues of child survival, 
maternal health, and contraception, while increasing outreach and coverage 
of a comprehensive package of reproductive and child health services by 
Government, industry and the voluntary non- government sector, working in 
partnership. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [05 MAY, 2000] 
Additionally 12 strategic themes are identified in the Policy. These are: 
(1) Decentralized planning and program implementation. 
(2) Convergence of service delivery at village levels. 
(3) Empowering women for improved health and nutrition. 
(4) Child Survival and Child Health. 
(5) Meeting the unmet needs for family welfare services. 
(6) Under-served population groups; 
Urban slums; 
Tribal communities, hill area population and displaced and 
migrant populations; 
Adolescents; 
Increased participation of men in planned parenthood. 
(7) Diverse health care provides. 
(8) Collaboration with and commitments from non-government 
organisations and the private sector. 
(9) Mainstream Indian Systems of Medicine and Homeopathy. 
 
(10) Contraceptive technology and research on reproductive and child 
health. 
(11) Providing for the Older Population. 
(12) Information, Education and Communication. 
The Policy envisages setting up of State/UT Commission on 
Population in addition to National Commission on Population to 
review and monitor implementation of strategies and action plan 
drawn in the Policy. 
(c) The long -term objective is to achieve population stabilisation by 
2045, at a level consistent with the requirements of sustainable economic 
growth, social development, and environmental protection. 
(d) and (e) No disincentives has been proposed in the National 
Population Policy, 2000 since the Policy affirms the commitment of 
government towards 
106 

[05 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the voluntary acceptance of small family norm by the ci tizens, through 
informed choice. 
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment has frozen the number of 
representatives in the Lok Sabha (on the basis of population) at 1971 Census 
levels. The freeze is currently valid until 2001, and has served as an incentive 
for St ate Governments to fearlessly pursue the agenda for population 
stabilisation. The Policy proposes to extend the freeze until 2026.

Technology Mission in the Departm ent of Family Welfare will be

(c) The long -term objective of the National Population Policy is to 
achieve Population stabilisation by 2045, at a level consistent with the 
requirements of sustainable economic growth, social development, and 
environmental protection. It envisages the following national Socio -
Demographic Goals to be achieved by 2010:—  
(!) Address the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health 
services, supplies and infrastructure. 
(2) Make school education up to age 14 free and compulsory, and 
reduce drop outs at primary and secondary school levels to below 
20 percent for both boys and girls. 
(3) Reduce infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1000 live births. 
(4) Reduce maternal mortality ratio to below 100 per 100,000 live 
births. 
(5) Achieve universal immunisation of children against all vaccine 
preventable diseases. 
(6) Promote delayed mar riage for girls, not earlier than age 18 and 
preferably after 20 years of age. 
(7) Achieve 80 percent institutional deliveries and 100 percent 
deliveries by trained persons.

(8) Achieve universal access to information/counseling, an d services 
for fertility regulation and contraception with a wide basket of 
choices. 
(9) Achieve 100 per cent registration of births, deaths, marriage and

(10) Contain the spread of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome 
(AIDS), and promote greater integrat ion between the management 
of reproductive trace infection (RTI) and sexually transmitted 
infractions (STI) and the National AIDS Control Organisation. 
(11) Prevent and control communicable diseases. 
(12) Integrate Indian System of Medicines (ISM) in the provision o f 
reproductive and child health services, and in reaching out to 
households. 
(13) Promote vigorously the small family to achieve replacement levels 
of TFR. 
(14) Bring about convergence in implementation of related social 
sector programmes so that family welfare beco mes a people 
centred programme.

Population Perspectives 
4317. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) the reasons for present day failure to control population growth in 
India; 
(b) whether compelling statutes rather than motivation would result in 
positive achievement; 
(c) if so, the changes in the statutes required and whether Government 
have any proposal to move in that direction; 
(d) the practice and principles adopted to control population in China 
and its success rate; 
(e) the advantages and achievements of population control programme 
during 1975 emergency and reasons for its discontinuance; and 
(f) the data on impact and extent of immigration on population growth 
of India since independence? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) to (f) For the 
country as a whole the achievement s under the family welfare programme 
have been quite substantial. Nine States and UTs including Kerala, Tamil 
Nadu and Goa have already achieved net replacement levels of fertility. 
Other States like Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Maharashtra are clos e 
to achieving it. However, some States are lagging behind primarily on 
account of slow achievement of socio-economic indicators. 
The population does not stabilise in response to Family Welfare 
Programmes alone. A large number of factors influence populati on growth 
rate and in turn are affected by it. Some of these factors are women's 
empowerment, 
110 

[05 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
women's status in the family, education particularly of women, etc. Actual 
success in containing the growth of population is dependent on : 
(i) Publicly stated support by the community leaders; 
(ii) Efficiency and accountability in the State Health System in 
ensuring effective delivery of high quality reproductive health 
care services to citizens; 
(iii) Education of women and care of the girl child; 
(iv) Employment of women and participation in the labour force; 
(v) Status of women etc. 
Reducing population growth and achieving population stabilisation is 
to be pursued as a multi-sectoral agenda. 
All these inputs have been only partial ly available for the Family 
Welfare Programme and this is the reason why the results so far have been 
only partial. 
The Family Welfare Programme in India is voluntary in nature, which 
enables a couple to adopt the family planning methods, best suited to th em, 
according to their choice, without any compulsion. Past experience shows 
that it is not feasible to enforce hard coercive measures for its promotion. 
In China, the Government has advocated a policy of one child per 
family. The Government has establishe d a set of incentives and disincentives 
to persuade couples to have only one child. China's annual growth rate of 
population is 0.9 (1995) and India's annual growth rate is 1.74. 
During the seventies, the Family Planning Programme was focused 
mainly on ter minal methods and the programme received a set back due to 
the rigid implementation of a target- based approach. The family welfare 
programme is now fully voluntary and the main effort of the Government has 
been to provide services on one hand and to encour age the citizens by 
information, education and communication on the other hand to use such 
services. 
In order to arrest the growth of population and achieve population 
stabilisation in the country at the earliest possible, Cabinet approved a 
National Population Policy —2000 during Feb. 2000. The National 
Population Policy was placed in the Rajya Sabha on 7th March, 2000.

4321. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD : Will the Minister of HEALTH  
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government propose to save the Indian society from most 
dreaded disease of AIDS; 
(b) if so, whether any preventive measure have been adopted; 
(c) whether any literature has been propagated through various media 
to create awareness among the people; and 
114 

[05 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, the broad features thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY W ELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM) : (a) to (d) The 
Government of India has launched the National AIDS Control Project -II in 
December, 1999 which aims to implement a comprehensive programme for 
the prevention and control of HIV/AIDS in the country. The main stra tegies 
of the programme are:—  
(i) Targeted Interventions to provide services and behaviour change 
communication to the most vulnerable and marginalised populations; 
(ii) Extensive awareness programmes for the general population and 
strengthening the blood safety measures; 
(iii) Low cost care for those already infected, 
(iv) Inter-sectoral collaboration to generate a multi sectoral response 
through various Ministeries and civil society; and 
(v) Strengthening institutions in India and make them capable of 
responding adequately to the epidemic. 
An important strategy is also to involve NGOs, especially in the 
Targeted Interventions, School AIDS Education, Counselling and Low Cost 
Community Care. 
Creating awareness is one of the most important thrust areas of the  
National AIDS Control Project- II. The focus of the strategy is on inter -
personal communication and reaching out to the rural poor and the 
population in the urban slums. Various programmes are being 
broadcast/telecast on All India Radio and Doordarshan. Po sters, pamphlets 
and other IEC material is developed in local languages. The field publicity 
units of the Directorate of Field Publicity and the Song & Drama Division of 
the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting are also being utilised to create 
awareness among people.

Vocational Training in Schools 
4354. DR. RAJA RAMANNA : Will th e Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have, for a long time, considered the need for 
vocational training in schools but the craze for university degrees has led to 
loss of good workmen in professions such as carpentry, welding, etc., and 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to consider steps to improve 
the quality of Indian goods, equal to or better than those of foreign countries, 
through a programme of training to produce highly trained vocational 
workers? 
THE MINIS TER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI JAYSINGRAO GAIKWAD PATIL) 
: (a) and (b) The need for diversifying secondary education by introducing 
knowledge and skills that may prepare students for remunerative work 
without the necessary  of having to go for higher education was emphasised 
by various experts and Education Commissions constituted by Government 
after independence. Keeping the above emphasis in view, vocational 
education was introduced at the secondary level as early as 1976 -77. The 
National Policy on Education, 1986 accorded high priority to the Vocational 
Education Programme. Accordingly, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of 
Vocationalisation of Secondary Education was launched in 1988. The 
objectives of the Scheme in essence are:—  
(i) to provide diversification of educational opportunities so as to 
enhance individual employability; 
(ii) to reduce mis-match between demand and supply of skilled 
manpower; 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [05 MAY, 2000] 
(iii) to provide an alternative to those pursuing higher education. 
Under the Scheme, financial assistance is extended to the States/UTs 
for implementation of vocational education programme at + 2 level. The 
Scheme also provides for financing innovative vocational programmes of 
shorter duration by Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs). 
The revision of vocational curriculum and instructional material to suit 
the requirements of the industry is being made from time to time. Linkages 
between schools and the industry are also being strengthened. 
Apprenticeship scheme has been extended to vocational pass -outs to 
strengthen the skills developed and to provide on the job experience. During 
the training, a stipend of Rs. 900/ - per month is paid for a period of one year 
to the trainees. Steps are being taken to improve the quality and popularise 
the Vocational Education Programme amongst students, parents and public 
at large.
